lessons.prologue: In AD 762, one hundred thousand builders raised a dazzling circular capital beside the River Tigris! Step through Baghdad’s four great gates, explore the Green Dome Palace at the City of Peace, and discover why this Silk Road crossroads dwarfed Anglo-Saxon towns in Britain.
lessons.blurb: In AD 762, one hundred thousand builders raised a dazzling circular capital beside the River Tigris! Step through Baghdad’s four great gates, explore the Green Dome Palace at the City of Peace, and discover why this Silk Road crossroads dwarfed Anglo-Saxon towns in Britain.

teacher_notes.primer: This opening Key Stage 2 enquiry introduces the rapid spread of early Islam from Mecca and Medina across Damascus, Cairo, Persia, and Spain before focusing on Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur’s decision to found Baghdad in AD 762. Primary pupils investigate why the fertile bend between the Tigris and Euphrates was a Silk Road crossroads, how 100,000 bricklayers built the 2km circular Round City (*Madinat al-Salam*), and how Baghdad’s nearly one million citizens around AD 900 contrasted starkly with Anglo-Saxon Britain’s small timber towns of 5,000–10,000 people.

items.question: On a history timeline, did AD 762 happen before or after the Romans left Britain around AD 410?
items.answer: After the Romans left Britain (more than 350 years later)
items.explanation: AD dates count upwards from AD 1, so AD 762 came three and a half centuries after Roman rule ended in Britain.

items.question: Why did so many ancient and medieval rulers choose to build capital cities beside major rivers?
items.answer: Rivers provided fresh drinking water, watered farm crops, and carried heavy trading boats
items.explanation: Before railways or lorries, river boats and canals were the fastest way to move food, bricks, and trade goods.

items.question: What was the famous network of overland trade routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, and the Mediterranean called?
items.answer: The Silk Roads (or Silk Road)
items.explanation: Caravans of camels and horses carried silk, spices, paper, glass, and ideas thousands of kilometres across Asia.

items.question: Which people ruled small kingdoms of wooden halls and farming villages across England around AD 900?
items.answer: The Anglo-Saxons (alongside Viking settlers in northern and eastern England)
items.explanation: Around AD 900, Anglo-Saxon Britain had small fortified *burh* towns of wooden houses rather than giant stone or brick cities.

items.question: What do historians mean when they call a group of many lands governed by one supreme ruler an "empire"?
items.answer: A large collection of countries, peoples, and cities united under a single ruler or government
items.explanation: In the early Islamic world, this vast empire was called a Caliphate and was led by a ruler known as a Caliph.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 610–762: Rapid Spread of Early Islam & Choosing the River Tigris
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] Beginning in **Mecca** and **Medina**, the faith of **Islam** spread swiftly across **Damascus**, **Cairo**, **Persia**, and **Spain**. In **AD 750**, the **Abbasid** family took charge of this vast empire, ruled by a **Caliph**. Twelve years later, in **AD 762**, **Caliph al-Mansur** searched for a safe, central place for his capital. He chose a fertile green bend on the **River Tigris**.

[1.2] Deep **canals** linked the **Tigris** straight to the **River Euphrates**, watering rich date palms and wheat fields. Round woven-reed **quffa** boats and river ships arrived carrying precious silk, spices, and porcelain. Camel caravans from China, India, and Africa also met at this busy crossroads. Al-Mansur knew peaceful trade would make his new city wealthy and strong.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 762–766: 100,000 Builders & the Round City of Peace
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Caliph al-Mansur gathered **100,000 bricklayers**, diggers, and craftworkers from many lands to raise **Baghdad**. Architects first traced a giant circle **two kilometres** across in flaming cotton seeds to test the layout. Builders then baked millions of mud bricks to construct thick **double walls** and a deep moat. Al-Mansur proudly called his circular capital **Madinat al-Salam**, meaning the **City of Peace**.

[1.4] Four guarded iron gates pierced the walls, named **Kufa**, **Basra**, **Khorasan**, and **Syria** towards **Damascus**. Straight covered market streets ran from each gate towards an open central ring. Right at the heart stood the **Great Mosque** beside the **Green Dome Palace**, rising high above the Tigris.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: One Million Citizens vs Anglo-Saxon Britain
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] Soon lively markets, bathhouses, and gardens spilled far beyond the original Round City walls. By **AD 900**, bustling Baghdad was home to nearly **one million people**! Residents strolled down **paved streets** beside cool **canals** and studied inside grand **libraries**.

[1.6] Meanwhile, life in **Anglo-Saxon Britain** around **AD 900** looked tiny by comparison. Even major English towns like **London** or **Winchester** held only **5,000 to 10,000 people**. Most British families lived inside smoky **timber huts** with thatched roofs along muddy lanes, showing how extraordinary Baghdad truly was!

tasks.model_answer: In AD 762, Caliph al-Mansur chose a fertile bend on the River Tigris for his circular capital because deep canals connected it straight to the River Euphrates, watering orchards and linking river boats with Silk Road camel caravans. Placing the Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace at the exact centre showed that faith and the Caliph’s peaceful rule anchored the whole world!

tasks.model_answer: Stepping through Baghdad’s tall brick gate after leaving my small timber town in Britain, I am amazed by the sheer scale of this City of Peace! Back home in Anglo-Saxon Winchester, fewer than 10,000 people live in smoky thatched timber huts beside muddy tracks. Here in Baghdad, nearly one million people stroll along clean paved streets, cross bridges over sparkling canals crowded with round quffa boats, trade pure gold dinars for Chinese silk, and read inside huge libraries!

tasks.question: Big Question: Why did Baghdad become the "Crossroads of the World" by AD 900, unlike towns in Britain?
tasks.starter: By AD 900, Baghdad had grown into the bustling Crossroads of the World because...
hints: Foundation Clues: Explain how geography (Tigris, Euphrates canals, and Silk Road caravans) brought wealth to Caliph al-Mansur’s capital.
Foundation Clues: Describe how 100,000 builders constructed the safe circular Round City (Madinat al-Salam) in AD 762.

tasks.model_answer: By AD 900, Baghdad had grown into the bustling Crossroads of the World because Caliph al-Mansur placed his AD 762 capital where Tigris and Euphrates canals met overland Silk Road caravans and sea ships from Asia and Africa. Protected by the double brick walls and four gates of Madinat al-Salam, trade and gold dinars funded paved streets, bathhouses, and grand libraries for nearly one million people. In contrast, divided Anglo-Saxon Britain had far smaller local trade networks, with towns of just 5,000 to 10,000 people living in thatched timber huts.

lessons.prologue: Step inside Baghdad’s legendary House of Wisdom, where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators worked side by side! Discover how cheap rag paper from Samarkand filled over a hundred bookshops, while Fatima al-Fihri and Queen Zubayda funded learning and desert wells.
lessons.blurb: Step inside Baghdad’s legendary House of Wisdom, where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators worked side by side! Discover how cheap rag paper from Samarkand filled over a hundred bookshops, while Fatima al-Fihri and Queen Zubayda funded learning and desert wells.

teacher_notes.primer: This second Key Stage 2 enquiry explores how Baghdad’s House of Wisdom (*Bayt al-Hikma*) under Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun united technological innovation with cultural exchange. Primary pupils trace how rag paper-making arrived from China via Samarkand to create over 100 bookshops (while Europe still scraped expensive calfskin parchment), how Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq rescued and tested Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit texts, and how women patrons Fatima al-Fihri (al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, AD 859) and Queen Zubayda (Hajj road wells) shaped the Golden Age.

source_context.Source A: Once Islamic craftworkers learned paper-making from Chinese makers via Samarkand, smooth rag paper replaced expensive animal-skin parchment for sacred texts, poetry, and science books. **Hinge Question:** Why did switching from calfskin parchment to cotton-and-rag paper let Baghdad open over 100 bookshops?
source_context.Source B: Inside Baghdad’s House of Wisdom, Christian physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq worked alongside Muslim and Jewish colleagues to translate Greek medical books by Galen and Hippocrates into clear Arabic. **Hinge Question:** What does Caliph al-Ma’mun hiring Christian, Jewish, and Muslim translators side by side reveal about Baghdad’s House of Wisdom?
source_context.Source C: Positioned halfway between China and Persia, the Silk Road oasis of Samarkand became famous in the AD 750s for fine rag paper that soon inspired paper mills in Baghdad, Damascus, and Spain. **Hinge Question:** How did Silk Road cities like Samarkand carry life-changing inventions as well as luxury silk and spices?
source_context.Source D: Building on Greek star catalogues translated into Arabic, astronomer al-Sufi observed the night sky himself to correct star positions and record the earliest note of the Andromeda Galaxy! **Hinge Question:** How does Source D prove Golden Age scholars tested and improved ancient Greek books rather than just copying them?

items.question: Name two of the Round City’s four gates and the two grand buildings right in the middle.
items.answer: Any two of Kufa, Basra, Khorasan, or Syria (towards Damascus); the Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace stood in the centre
items.explanation: Straight covered streets led from the four outer gates into the central park around the palace and mosque.

items.question: Around AD 900, how did Baghdad’s population compare with major towns in Anglo-Saxon Britain like London or Winchester?
items.answer: Baghdad had nearly one million people, while big Anglo-Saxon towns held only 5,000 to 10,000 people
items.explanation: Most families in Anglo-Saxon Britain lived in thatched timber huts, while Baghdad boasted paved streets, canals, and libraries.

items.question: What were round woven-reed quffa boats and Abbasid gold dinars used for in Baghdad?
items.answer: Quffa boats carried goods along the River Tigris, and pure gold dinars paid merchants across long-distance trade routes
items.explanation: Reliable river transport and trusted gold coins helped turn Baghdad into the Crossroads of the World.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 786–833: Harun al-Rashid, Al-Ma’mun & the Paper Revolution
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] Under **Caliph Harun al-Rashid** and his son **Caliph al-Ma'mun**, bustling Baghdad became a magnet for curious thinkers. Together they expanded a royal library into the famous **House of Wisdom**, or **Bayt al-Hikma**. Meanwhile, craftworkers via the Silk Road city of **Samarkand** learned the Chinese secret of **paper-making**. Baghdad watermills beat old cotton and linen rags into smooth, cheap sheets of paper.

[2.2] Across **Europe**, scribes still scraped costly **calfskin parchment**, needing whole cattle herds for one big book! Cheap rag paper transformed Baghdad and sparked over **100 bustling bookshops** in the **Paper Sellers' Market**. Readers browsed poetry, history, and star charts written in neat Arabic ink.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 830–900: The Translation Movement & Hunayn ibn Ishaq
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] Caliph al-Ma'mun sent keen messengers to Constantinople, Persia, and India to buy rare ancient scrolls. Inside the House of Wisdom, this bold **Translation Movement** rescued fragile books before they crumbled away. **Muslim**, **Christian**, and **Jewish** scholars worked side by side translating **Greek**, **Persian**, and **Sanskrit** books into **Arabic**.

[2.4] The star translator was **Hunayn ibn Ishaq**, a gifted Christian doctor fluent in Greek, Syriac, and Arabic. Stories tell that Caliph al-Ma'mun paid Hunayn the weight of every finished medical book in gold! Crucially, Baghdad's scholars never copied old writers blindly. Instead, they tested every idea, fixed errors, and added fresh discoveries.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 800–900: Visionary Women Patrons — Fatima al-Fihri & Queen Zubayda
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] Generous women across the Islamic world also shaped this Golden Age as visionary **patrons**. In **AD 859**, **Fatima al-Fihri** spent her family inheritance in the Moroccan city of **Fez**. She founded **al-Qarawiyyin**, a grand mosque and teaching college that still welcomes eager students today! Learners travelled to Fez to study mathematics, star maps, grammar, and law.

[2.6] Earlier in Baghdad, **Queen Zubayda**, wife of Harun al-Rashid, funded a giant desert water project. Thirsty pilgrims walking the scorching **Hajj road** to Mecca often ran low on fresh water. Zubayda paid stonemasons to dig deep **wells** and reservoirs along that trail, saving thousands of travellers!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 820–1206: Zero, Algebra, Astrolabes & the Elephant Clock
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] Working in Baghdad's House of Wisdom, mathematician **Muhammad al-Khwarizmi** championed **Hindu-Arabic numerals** from **0 to 9**. Including **zero**, called **sifr** in Arabic, made big sums far clearer than clumsy Roman numerals! His landmark book **al-Jabr** gave the world **algebra**, while his own name gave us **algorithm**.

[3.2] Skilled makers like **Mariam al-Asturlabi** crafted intricate brass **astrolabes** engraved with star maps. Travellers held up an astrolabe to check prayer times, sail oceans, and find **Mecca**. Later, master engineer **al-Jazari** built his marvellous **Elephant Water Clock** to mark each half hour. Hidden water floats inside the elephant made mechanical figures whirl, chirp, and clash loud brass cymbals!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 965–1040: Ibn al-Haytham’s Light Proof & Free Bimaristans
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] For centuries, ancient Greek writers claimed invisible rays shot out of human eyes to see things. Scientist **Ibn al-Haytham** doubted that idea and tested light inside a pitch-dark room with a tiny pinhole. Inside his pinhole **camera obscura**, he proved that light travels in **straight lines** directly into our eyes! His careful experiments inspired modern cameras and eyeglasses.

[3.4] Islamic cities also opened free teaching hospitals called **bimaristans** for rich and poor citizens alike. Each **bimaristan** had separate **clean wards**, cooling fountains, and a stocked **pharmacy**. Patients even received clean clothes and pocket money to rest at home after recovering!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900–1013: Master Doctors Al-Razi & Al-Zahrawi
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] Before choosing a site for Baghdad's hospital, chief doctor **al-Razi** hung fresh meat across different districts. He picked the spot where the meat rotted slowest because the air there was cleanest! By writing careful bedside notes, al-Razi became the first doctor to distinguish **measles** from **smallpox**. Trained nurses served healthy meals while students learned on the wards.

[3.6] Far west in Spain, royal surgeon **al-Zahrawi** wrote a thirty-volume illustrated medical guide around **AD 1000**. He invented over **200 surgical tools**, including forceps, scalpels, and delicate bone saws still used today. Al-Zahrawi even discovered that **catgut stitches** dissolve safely inside the body as wounds heal!

tasks.starter: Inspecting Sources A, B, and C shows how much modern life owes to Golden Age thinkers because...
hints: Foundation Clues: Explain how al-Khwarizmi’s book in Source A gave us algebra, algorithms, and 0–9 numbers with zero.

tasks.model_answer: Inspecting Sources A, B, and C shows how much modern life owes to Golden Age thinkers because Source A’s page by Muhammad al-Khwarizmi gave us 0–9 numerals with zero, algebra, and the step-by-step algorithms running every phone and computer today! Source B’s brass astrolabe worked like an early pocket star calculator for telling time and navigating oceans. Finally, Source C’s clear diagrams of over 200 surgical tools by al-Zahrawi ensured smiths and surgeons used safe forceps, scalpels, and dissolving catgut stitches!

tasks.question: Explain how Ibn al-Haytham and doctor al-Razi used clever experiments instead of guesswork.
tasks.starter: Both Ibn al-Haytham and Baghdad doctor al-Razi proved the power of real scientific testing because...
hints: Foundation Clues: Describe how Ibn al-Haytham used a dark pinhole room (camera obscura) to prove light enters our eyes in straight lines.
Foundation Clues: Describe how al-Razi hung fresh meat around Baghdad to pick the cleanest-air hospital site.
Scholar Challenge: Add how al-Razi’s careful bedside notes made him the first doctor to tell measles apart from smallpox!
tasks.model_answer: Both Ibn al-Haytham and Baghdad doctor al-Razi proved the power of real scientific testing because neither scholar accepted old claims without evidence. When ancient Greek books claimed rays shot out of human eyes, Ibn al-Haytham built a pitch-dark pinhole camera obscura and proved light actually travels in straight lines into our eyes! Similarly, al-Razi hung fresh meat across Baghdad to build his bimaristan where meat rotted slowest in clean air, and kept detailed bedside notes to distinguish measles from smallpox.

tasks.question: Big Question: Which Golden Age breakthrough changed our modern world the most — maths, optics, or medicine?
tasks.starter: Although maths, optics, and medicine all transformed human life, I think the biggest Golden Age breakthrough was...
hints: Foundation Clues: Compare al-Khwarizmi’s 0–9 numerals, zero (sifr), algebra, and algorithms with Mariam al-Asturlabi’s astrolabes.
Foundation Clues: Weigh up Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura light proof and free bimaristan hospitals.
Scholar Challenge: Reach a clear judgement explaining how your chosen breakthrough connects to the other two in modern life!
tasks.model_answer: Although maths, optics, and medicine all transformed human life, I think al-Khwarizmi’s mathematics changed our modern world the most because every other science depends on it! His Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9 including zero, sifr), algebra, and step-by-step algorithms power modern computers, engineering, and hospital machines alike. Even so, Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura gave us eyeglasses and cameras, while free bimaristans, al-Razi’s clinical notes, and al-Zahrawi’s 200 surgical tools and dissolving catgut stitches created the blueprint for modern healthcare!

teacher_notes.primer: This fourth Key Stage 2 enquiry explores Baghdad's global trade networks between c. AD 850 and 1000. Primary pupils trace overland Silk Road camel caravans stopping every 30 km at fortified caravanserais, maritime dhow voyages from Basra across the Indian Ocean using astrolabes, and early paper cheques (sakk). Crucially, pupils connect Baghdad directly to British history through Abbasid silver dirham hoards found around Viking Jorvik (York) and Anglo-Saxon King Offa of Mercia's gold imitation dinar.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 850–1000: Covered Bazaars, Silk Caravans & Roadside Caravanserais
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] Baghdad sat right where Asia, Africa, and Europe met, making its markets world famous. Shaded covered **bazaars**, called **souks**, smelled of Indian pepper, green cardamom, and sweet cinnamon. Stalls gleamed with Chinese silk, white porcelain bowls, Persian carpets, and delicate blown glass. Long **caravans** of two-humped camels carried these treasures across hot **Silk Road** desert trails.

[4.2] Every thirty kilometres along the trail stood a walled roadside inn called a **caravanserai**. Thick brick walls and locked gates sheltered merchants from desert bandits while camels drank well water. Traders shared hot spiced stews and travel news by firelight before marching onward at dawn.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 850–1000: Indian Ocean Dhow Ships & Paper Sakk Cheques
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] River boats also carried crates down the Tigris to the busy port of **Basra**. Sailors loaded wooden **dhow** ships built from planks stitched tightly with coconut rope. Tall triangular sails caught ocean winds across the **Indian Ocean** towards India and China. Captains steered safely across open water at night by measuring star heights with brass **astrolabes**.

[4.4] Carrying heavy sacks of gold and silver coins across deserts or seas risked pirate attacks. Clever Baghdad bankers solved this by writing signed paper payment slips called a **sakk**. Merchants cashed their paper **sakk** safely in distant cities, giving English our modern word **cheque**!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 774–1000: Viking Silver Dirhams in Jorvik & King Offa’s Gold Coin
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Amazingly, silver coins struck for Baghdad’s caliphs travelled north to snowy **Scandinavia** and **Britain**! Pure Abbasid silver **dirhams**, stamped with Arabic script, flowed along Russian rivers with fur traders. **Vikings** prized this trusted Islamic silver and buried shining hoards near **Jorvik**, modern **York**. Archaeologists have dug up thousands of Baghdad silver dirhams from Scandinavian and British soil!

[4.6] Even earlier, Anglo-Saxon **King Offa of Mercia** admired golden Islamic coins reaching western Europe. Around **AD 774**, Offa minted a famous gold coin copying an Abbasid Arabic **dinar**! His coin copied swirling Arabic script beside Offa’s name, proving Baghdad’s trade reached medieval Britain.

tasks.model_answer: Crossing thousands of miles of desert and sea was dangerous for medieval traders, so rulers built walled brick caravanserais every thirty kilometres along the Silk Road. Behind locked gates, camel caravans rested safely from desert bandits, drank fresh well water, and shared news. In addition, Baghdad bankers invented signed paper payment slips called a sakk — giving us our English word cheque — so merchants could travel without carrying heavy sacks of gold coins!

tasks.model_answer: Between AD 850 and 1000, Baghdad's traders linked three continents, and astonishing coin clues even connect them to Britain. Eastwards, camel caravans trekked the Silk Road to China while wooden dhow ships sailed from Basra across the Indian Ocean for pepper, cardamom, and pearls. Northwards, pure Abbasid silver dirhams flowed along Russian rivers to Viking traders, who buried thousands of them in hoards across Scandinavia and near Jorvik (York). Even Anglo-Saxon King Offa of Mercia minted a gold coin around AD 774 copying an Arabic dinar!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: Cool Courtyard Houses, Windcatchers & Public Hammams
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] Summer afternoons in Iraq blazed fiercely hot, yet Baghdad’s builders kept family homes remarkably cool. Thick brick walls surrounded shaded inner **courtyards** splashed by stone fountains and fragrant orange trees. Above the roofs rose tall **windcatcher** towers, called **badgirs**, facing straight into the breeze. These clever towers scooped cool outdoor air down indoors while pushing hot air outside!

[5.2] Cleanliness and fresh water mattered deeply in daily Islamic life before prayers and family meals. Every neighbourhood had steamed public bathhouses called **hammams**, with hot and cool tiled rooms. Bathers scrubbed with scented olive-oil **soap** bars and splashed sweet **rosewater** onto clean linen robes.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: Citrus Orchards, Spiced Kitchens & Geometric Mosque Art
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Canal waterwheels irrigated lush orchards around Baghdad bursting with exciting new crops from Asia. Farmers grew tangy **lemons**, sweet **oranges**, purple **aubergines**, fresh green **spinach**, and ruby **pomegranates**. Cooks simmered spiced stews with crushed **almonds** and **cane sugar**, served on metallic **lustreware** bowls.

[5.4] Inside mosques, artists avoided carving human or animal statues so worshippers honoured God alone. Instead, craftworkers used brass rulers and compasses to tile dazzling eight-pointed **geometric** star mosaics. Flowing leaf vines called **arabesque** curled smoothly beside sacred **Arabic calligraphy** from the Qur’an. Every repeating star pattern reminded viewers of the endless order and beauty of creation.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: Silk Tiraz Robes, Glass Mosque Lamps & Shatranj Chess
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] Beyond mosques, skilled workshops filled Baghdad’s homes with bright silk textiles and glowing glasswork. Royal looms wove luxury silk robes trimmed with embroidered Arabic name bands called **tiraz**. Master glassblowers also gilded enamelled **mosque lamps** inscribed with glowing verses about divine light.

[5.6] When evening breezes cooled the courtyard, families gathered on woven carpets for poetry and riddles. Happy guests sipped chilled fruit syrups sweetened with sugar and fragrant drops of rosewater. Best loved of all was **shatranj**, an ancient strategy board game that became modern **chess**! Clever players cried *Shah mat*, meaning the king is helpless, giving English our word **checkmate**!

tasks.model_answer: Even though Iraqi summers were scorching hot, families in Baghdad lived comfortably and ate well because clever builders surrounded shaded fountain courtyards with thick walls and tall windcatcher towers that scooped cool breezes indoors. Outside the city walls, waterwheels irrigated orchards growing lemons, oranges, aubergines, spinach, pomegranates, almonds, and sweet cane sugar!

tasks.model_answer: Exploring homes, kitchens, mosques, and workshops in AD 900 Baghdad proves early Islamic civilisation was inventive, clean, artistic, and globally connected. Builders engineered natural windcatcher cooling and piped water to tiled hammams where people washed with soap and rosewater. Canal orchards filled kitchens with lemons, oranges, aubergines, spinach, and cane sugar. Meanwhile, artists used geometry and calligraphy to create eight-pointed star mosaics, lustreware bowls, silk tiraz robes, and ceramic shatranj chess sets enjoyed by families at home!

items.question: Why did Caliph al-Mansur choose the River Tigris in AD 762 for his Round City of Baghdad?
items.answer: Fertile land watered by canals to the Euphrates placed Baghdad right at the crossroads of land and sea routes

items.question: How did Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars like Hunayn ibn Ishaq work together inside the House of Wisdom?
items.answer: They translated Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit books into Arabic onto affordable Samarkand paper

items.question: How did al-Khwarizmi and free bimaristan hospitals improve maths and healthcare?

narrative_blocks.title: January–February AD 1258: Hulagu Khan & the Mongol Siege of Baghdad
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] Over centuries, the huge Abbasid Empire slowly split into smaller rival kingdoms. Baghdad remained a proud centre of learning, yet its weakened army could not guard borders. In **January 1258**, a vast **Mongol army** led by **Hulagu Khan** marched from Central Asia. Hundreds of thousands of Mongol horsemen surrounded Baghdad along both banks of the River Tigris.

[6.2] Mongol engineers built giant wooden **trebuchets** that hurled heavy boulders at Baghdad’s brick walls. In **February 1258**, Hulagu’s troops stormed through the broken walls and sacked the city. Fires destroyed palaces, canals, and the **House of Wisdom**, ending Abbasid rule in Baghdad.

narrative_blocks.title: Cairo, Córdoba & Toledo: Why Golden Age Knowledge Survived
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] Did the **Golden Age** vanish forever in **1258** when Baghdad’s famous library burned down? Thankfully not, because paper copies already sat safely in **Cairo**, **Damascus**, and **Samarkand**! Far west in Islamic Spain, called **Al-Andalus**, **Córdoba** shone with street lamps and seventy libraries. Spanish Muslim rulers also built the carved arches and marble courtyards of the **Alhambra** palace.

[6.4] Crucially, the Spanish city of **Toledo** became Europe’s greatest bridge for sharing Arabic science. Muslim, Jewish, and Christian translators worked together turning **al-Khwarizmi**, **Ibn al-Haytham**, and **Ibn Sina** into **Latin**. Those rescued books reached European universities and helped spark the scientific rebirth called the **Renaissance**!

narrative_blocks.title: From 1258 to Today: Arabic Words & Ideas in Our Everyday Lives
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Even today, Golden Age breakthroughs shape your classroom, hospital, and pocket phone every single day! Writing digits **0 to 9**, solving **algebra**, or running a computer **algorithm** uses Baghdad’s maths. **Ibn al-Haytham’s** dark-room light experiments led straight to spectacles, microscopes, and smartphone cameras. Clean hospital wards, busy pharmacies, and surgical tools also build upon early Islamic medicine.

[6.6] You even speak everyday Arabic words whenever you say **zero**, **chemistry**, **sugar**, **lemon**, or **orange**! Cosy home words like **sofa** and **cotton** also travelled into English through Arabic trade. Though Hulagu’s siege shattered Baghdad’s walls in **1258**, Golden Age ideas changed our world forever.

key_individuals.name: Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (AD 714–775)
key_individuals.role: Second Abbasid Caliph & Visionary Founder of the Round City of Baghdad
key_individuals.origins: Born into the Abbasid family descended from the Prophet Muhammad’s uncle al-Abbas; searched Iraq personally in AD 762 for a breezy, fertile riverside crossroads.
key_individuals.significance: Chose a strategic bend on the River Tigris linked by canals to the Euphrates and laid out Madinat al-Salam ("City of Peace") as a geometric circle two kilometres wide.
achievements: Gathered around 100,000 builders, bricklayers, and surveyors in AD 762 to raise Baghdad’s double brick walls, deep moat, and four great gates.
Placed the Green Dome Palace and Great Mosque right at the heart of the Round City, facing roads towards Basra, Kufa, Khorasan, and Damascus.
Started the royal palace library collection of Persian, Greek, and Sanskrit books that blossomed into Baghdad’s famous House of Wisdom.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Traced Baghdad’s giant circular street plan onto the ground with lines of cotton seeds soaked in oil and lit them with fire so he could inspect the layout from above!

key_individuals.name: Caliph Harun al-Rashid & Queen Zubayda (c. AD 766–831)
key_individuals.role: Fifth Abbasid Caliph & Royal Patroness of Scholars, Hospitals & Desert Water Engineering
key_individuals.origins: Royal cousins who presided over Baghdad at the height of its wealth and fame, remembered in history books and The Thousand and One Nights alike.
key_individuals.significance: Turned Baghdad into a magnet for global translators, doctors, poets, and diplomats while funding major public works that served ordinary travellers.
achievements: Harun al-Rashid expanded the royal House of Wisdom, founded Baghdad’s first free bimaristan hospital, and sent diplomatic gifts — including an Asian elephant and brass water clock — to Emperor Charlemagne!
Queen Zubayda funded the 1,400-kilometre Darb Zubayda desert road from Iraq to Mecca, paying engineers to blast rock cisterns, wells, and milestones for thirsty pilgrims.
Patronised paper mills, silk tiraz workshops, and pure gold dinar and silver dirham mints trusted from China to northern Europe.
key_individuals.key_distinction: When engineers warned Queen Zubayda that carving desert wells would cost a fortune, she famously replied to build it even if every single pickaxe blow cost a coin of pure gold!

key_individuals.name: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. AD 780–850)
key_individuals.role: House of Wisdom Mathematician, Astronomer & "Father of Algebra"
key_individuals.origins: Born around Khwarazm near the Aral Sea in Central Asia before moving to Baghdad under Caliph al-Ma’mun to lead maths and astronomy research in the House of Wisdom.
key_individuals.significance: Revolutionised world mathematics by championing place-value Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9, including sifr / zero) and inventing step-by-step equation-solving.
achievements: Wrote Kitab al-Jabr around AD 820 to help people calculate inheritances, land measurements, and canal digging — giving every language the word "algebra"!
Explained how zero (sifr) works as a place-holder so merchants and scientists could add, subtract, and multiply far faster than with Roman numerals.
Calculated accurate star tables and revised world maps with seventy fellow geographers; the Latin spelling of his name (Algoritmi) gave us "algorithm"!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Every single search engine, video game, and smartphone app running on "algorithms" today carries the name of this 9th-century Baghdad mathematician!

key_individuals.name: Fatima al-Fihri & Mariam al-Asturlabi (9th–10th Century AD)
key_individuals.role: Pioneering Female Patron of Learning & Master Maker of Brass Astrolabes
key_individuals.origins: Fatima al-Fihri grew up in an educated merchant family moving from Kairouan to Fez in Morocco; a century later, Mariam al-Asturlabi trained in precision brass engineering in Syria.
key_individuals.significance: Prove that women played vital roles in early Islamic scholarship and scientific instrument-making, funding seats of higher learning and crafting complex sky computers.
achievements: In AD 859, Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found al-Qarawiyyin in Fez — still operating in Morocco over 1,160 years later as the world’s oldest continually running degree-granting institution!
Mariam al-Asturlabi hand-engraved intricate brass planispheric astrolabes so accurate that the ruler of Aleppo hired her at his royal court.
Enabled sailors on Indian Ocean dhows, desert travellers, and astronomers to tell time by the stars and find the exact direction of Mecca.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Modern astronomers named main-belt asteroid 7060 Al-Ijliya in honour of Mariam al-Asturlabi’s dazzling brass star-mapping instruments!

key_individuals.name: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, c. AD 965–1040)
key_individuals.role: Physicist, Astronomer, Pioneer of Optics & Champion of the Scientific Method
key_individuals.origins: Born in the Iraqi port city of Basra during the Islamic Golden Age and later worked beside Cairo’s great libraries and mosques.
key_individuals.significance: Overturned ancient Greek guesses that invisible beams shot out of human eyes, using dark-room experiments to prove light travels in straight lines into our eyes.
achievements: Built a darkened pinhole chamber (al-bayt al-muzlim — Latin camera obscura) showing how light rays pass through a tiny hole to project an upside-down image.
Wrote the seven-volume Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir), explaining reflection, refraction, rainbows, lenses, and how the eye’s cornea and optic nerve work.
Insisted scientists must doubt untested claims and check every idea with repeatable experiments — a cornerstone of the modern scientific method!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Known in Latin Europe as "Alhazen", his pinhole dark-room experiments paved the way for reading glasses, telescopes, microscopes, and every camera on Earth!

key_individuals.name: Al-Razi & Al-Zahrawi (9th–10th Century AD)
key_individuals.role: Chief Baghdad Hospital Physician & Pioneering Surgeon of Al-Andalus
key_individuals.origins: Al-Razi (Rhazes) directed major bimaristan hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, while al-Zahrawi (Albucasis) practised surgery near Córdoba in Islamic Spain.
key_individuals.significance: Transformed medieval medicine from superstition into careful clinical observation, hygienic hospital care, and illustrated surgical training.
achievements: Before choosing where to build Baghdad’s new hospital, al-Razi hung fresh meat around the city and picked the spot where it rotted slowest — proving the air there was cleanest!
Al-Razi wrote the first clear medical guide telling measles apart from smallpox and compiled gigantic medical encyclopaedias used for centuries.

Al-Zahrawi wrote a thirty-volume medical guide illustrating over 200 surgical instruments — forceps, scalpels, bone saws — and pioneered internal stitches made from natural catgut that dissolved harmlessly as patients healed!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Translated into Latin in Spain, al-Razi’s and al-Zahrawi’s illustrated books trained European doctors and surgeons for more than five hundred years!
